The MMA consists of two nested closed hexagon ring resonators made of copper on top of a metallic ground plane, separated by a 0.7 mm thick dielectric FR4 substrate.
The MMA has two absorption peaks at 8.1 GHz and 10.7 GHz, with absorption rates of 0.95 and 0.94 respectively for TE polarization, and 0.94 and 0.90 for TM polarization.
The symmetrical structure of the MMA allows it to have almost the same response to both TE and TM polarizations, making it polarization-independent.
The metallic ground plane is responsible for the magnetic resonance by exciting an anti-parallel surface current to that of the top layer.
Adjusting the outer ring radius r_out only affects the location of the lower resonance frequency, while the higher resonance frequency remains almost unchanged.
Changing the substrate length a and thickness h does not significantly affect the resonance frequencies, but rather impacts the resonant strength or minimum reflection coefficient (S11).
The final optimized dimensions of the MMA unit cell are: a = 8.4 mm, r1 = 2.6 mm, w = 0.3 mm, r_out = 3.2 mm, and h = 0.7 mm.
The MMA design is a good candidate for high-performance absorbers with potential applications in radar stealth technology.
The Master and Slave boundaries in the x and y directions are used to simulate the periodic structure of the MMA, while the Floquet Ports in the z direction are used to define the excitation.
Metamaterial absorbers can create new materials with properties not found in nature, which makes them useful for applications like radar stealth technology.
Each of the two nested hexagon rings is responsible for one of the two resonance frequencies of the MMA.
The absorption is defined as A = 1 - R - T, where R = |S11|^2 represents reflection and T = |S21|^2 represents transmission.
Due to the metal ground plane, the transmission is zero, so the absorption is calculated as A = 1 - |S11|^2.
The top layer of the MMA is mainly responsible for the electric resonance, while the bottom layer is responsible for the magnetic resonance.
The MMA design presented in this paper is a simple and efficient approach to achieve a dual-band and polarization-independent absorber in the GHz regime.
